chapterTitle: Do Nudges Last Forever? Perhaps in Sweden
focus: Sweden's premium-pension system shows how an initial campaign for active choice can shape portfolios for years. Too many funds, promotional advertising, and inertia made early decisions persist after attention disappeared.
coreClaim: A one-time nudge can have durable consequences when later review is rare and switching is not actively prompted.

centralConcept.name: persistent choice architecture
centralConcept.plainDefinition: An initial default or active-choice campaign continues to affect outcomes because people seldom revisit the decision.
centralConcept.whyItMatters: Architects must judge a design by long-run portfolio quality and review behavior, not only first-day engagement.

keyClaims: Sweden launched its premium-pension fund market in 2000.
A booklet presented 456 funds from 72 companies to about four million savers.
Nearly two thirds initially chose actively after a major campaign.
Fund advertising emphasized salience more than fees or diversification.
Active portfolios were often riskier and more expensive than the default.
New cohorts became far less likely to choose actively as promotion faded.
Both active choices and delegation became sticky.

namedExamples.label: Swedish Premium Pension Agency / 2000 fund launch
namedExamples.summary: Around four million Swedes received a catalog covering 456 funds managed by 72 companies and could allocate savings among one to five funds. The government campaign encouraged active selection rather than passive use of the default.
namedExamples.teachesWhat: A campaign can overpower a default by framing active choice as the responsible action.
hardSpecifics: catalog sent to about four million people in 2000

namedExamples.label: Henrik Cronqvist and Richard Thaler / Swedish portfolio analysis
namedExamples.summary: Cronqvist and Thaler compared actively selected portfolios with the government default. Active choosers tended toward higher fees, more concentrated risk, and stronger home bias, while advertising predicted fund flows.
namedExamples.teachesWhat: More active choice does not guarantee a better portfolio when the menu and marketing are difficult.
hardSpecifics: 2004 analysis of the Swedish premium-pension launch
active portfolios were costlier and less diversified than the default

namedExamples.label: Seventh AP Fund / Premium Savings Fund
namedExamples.summary: Savers who made no selection entered the state-run Premium Savings Fund managed by AP7. The low-cost diversified default later evolved toward an age-adjusted AP7 Såfa structure.
namedExamples.teachesWhat: A delegated default can outperform unaided active selection when it is designed as a real product rather than a penalty box.
hardSpecifics: default managed by Sweden's Seventh AP Fund
later AP7 Såfa allocation becomes more bond-heavy with age

hardEdge: The lesson is not that active choice is always bad or that a government fund is always superior. It is that engagement counts are a poor success metric when the choice is complex, advertising is salient, and portfolios remain untouched for decades.
voiceCues: uses one national system as a chapter-length case
tracks behavior across cohorts and years
uses an inertia metaphor to close

testableFacts.claim: Sweden's 2000 launch presented 456 funds from 72 companies to about four million savers.
testableFacts.becauseMechanism: This mechanism operates because the large catalog made the premium-pension allocation an unusually complex mass-market choice.
testableFacts.commonError: Participants chose among a short curated list of fewer than ten funds.
testableFacts.errorIsWhy: The launch menu contained hundreds of funds.

testableFacts.claim: Cronqvist and Thaler found actively selected Swedish portfolios were generally costlier and less diversified than the default.
testableFacts.becauseMechanism: This mechanism operates because advertising and recent returns attracted attention toward concentrated, higher-fee options.
testableFacts.commonError: Active choosers reliably earned a diversification advantage over delegators.
testableFacts.errorIsWhy: The observed portfolio characteristics pointed in the opposite direction.

testableFacts.claim: The Seventh AP Fund managed the Premium Savings Fund for people who made no active selection.
testableFacts.becauseMechanism: This mechanism operates because a centralized default provided an investable allocation when savers delegated the decision.
testableFacts.commonError: Nonchoosers left their premium-pension contributions in cash.
testableFacts.errorIsWhy: Their money entered the state-run default fund.

testableFacts.claim: Almost two thirds of eligible savers made an active choice in the launch year.
testableFacts.becauseMechanism: This mechanism operates because government communication and private advertising framed active management as expected and responsible.
testableFacts.commonError: The presence of a default caused nearly everyone to delegate immediately.
testableFacts.errorIsWhy: The campaign against passive acceptance outweighed the default for the initial cohort.

testableFacts.claim: Fund companies spent about 65 million US dollars advertising during the initial Swedish choice round, with spending falling below 10 million by 2003.
testableFacts.becauseMechanism: This mechanism operates because the collapse in promotion reduced salience and coincided with much lower active choice among later entrants.
testableFacts.commonError: The menu attracted the same engagement without marketing.
testableFacts.errorIsWhy: Active selection fell sharply as campaign intensity faded.

testableFacts.claim: The original system let savers divide their allocation among one to five funds.
testableFacts.becauseMechanism: This mechanism operates because the rule encouraged portfolio construction from a hundreds-fund menu rather than one simple selection.
testableFacts.commonError: Every active saver had to select exactly one fund.
testableFacts.errorIsWhy: The design explicitly permitted multiple funds up to five.

testableFacts.claim: Later cohorts entered the default at much higher rates than the 2000 cohort.
testableFacts.becauseMechanism: This mechanism operates because with less advertising and public attention, inaction again became the path of least resistance.
testableFacts.commonError: The culture of active pension management strengthened automatically over time.
testableFacts.errorIsWhy: New-entrant active choice declined after launch.

testableFacts.claim: Early active choices remained sticky even after the original promotional environment disappeared.
testableFacts.becauseMechanism: This mechanism operates because review required attention and effort, so savers treated a one-time portfolio as a set-and-forget decision.
testableFacts.commonError: Active choosers continuously rebalance because they rejected delegation once.
testableFacts.errorIsWhy: Initial activeness did not imply ongoing monitoring.

testableFacts.claim: An age-adjusted default reduces equity exposure as retirement approaches.
testableFacts.becauseMechanism: This mechanism operates because a lifecycle allocation automatically changes risk when the saver may not revisit the portfolio.
testableFacts.commonError: A good retirement default should hold the same asset mix at every age.
testableFacts.errorIsWhy: Capacity to absorb market loss changes with the remaining investment horizon.

paraphraseNotes: Sweden's premium-pension launch is a long experiment in competing nudges. In 2000, about four million people received material describing 456 funds from 72 companies and could allocate among one to five. A government campaign and roughly 65 million dollars in fund advertising encouraged active management, and almost two thirds selected portfolios rather than enter the Premium Savings Fund. Henrik Cronqvist and Richard Thaler's analysis found that engagement did not produce superior construction. Active portfolios tended to carry higher fees, more concentration, and stronger home bias than the low-cost diversified default managed by the Seventh AP Fund. Advertising and recent performance attracted flows, while relevant characteristics were harder to evaluate. The launch effect did not renew itself. Advertising fell below 10 million dollars by 2003, later cohorts overwhelmingly delegated, and people on both paths rarely revisited their status. A saver who actively chose once did not become a continuously attentive manager. The persistence cuts both ways: an effective default can protect inattentive savers, while a poor early portfolio can remain frozen long after its rationale disappears. AP7's later age-adjusted Såfa structure treats the default as a product that must evolve with the saver rather than a holding pen. The evaluation standard is therefore long-run fees, diversification, risk, and review—not the number of people induced to click in year one. Grounding anchors: 456 funds from 72 fund companies; catalog sent to about four million people in 2000; 2004 analysis of the Swedish premium-pension launch; active portfolios were costlier and less diversified than the default; default managed by Sweden's Seventh AP Fund; later AP7 Såfa allocation becomes more bond-heavy with age.
